# sysutils_package (Resource)

Installs, upgrades, pins to a version or removes an OS package with the host's package manager: `apt-get` on Debian and Ubuntu, `dnf` or `yum` on Fedora and RHEL-like distributions, `apk` on Alpine. The installed version is read from the package database (`dpkg-query`, `rpm -q`, `apk info`), so packages installed, upgraded or removed outside Terraform show up as drift. Commands run without a shell and without prompts. Requires root privileges.

It covers the same ground as Ansible's `package`, `apt`, `dnf` and `apk` modules for a single package.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Installed if missing. On a fresh image, refresh the package index first.
resource "sysutils_package" "nginx" {
  name         = "nginx"
  update_cache = true
}

# Kept at the newest version in the package index.
resource "sysutils_package" "ca_certificates" {
  name  = "ca-certificates"
  state = "latest"
}

# Pinned to an exact version: upgrades made outside Terraform are reverted.
resource "sysutils_package" "tree" {
  name    = "tree"
  version = "2.1.1-2ubuntu3"
  manager = "apt"
}

# Removed if installed.
resource "sysutils_package" "telnet" {
  name  = "telnet"
  state = "absent"
}

# Installed before Terraform managed it: keep it when the resource is
# destroyed.
resource "sysutils_package" "openssh_server" {
  name              = "openssh-server"
  remove_on_destroy = false
}

output "nginx_version" {
  value = sysutils_package.nginx.installed_version
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the package, such as `"nginx"`. 1 to 128 letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `+` or `-`, starting with a letter or digit; with apt, lowercase and at least 2 characters, as Debian requires. Architecture qualifiers, version constraints, globs, file paths and virtual `provides` are not accepted. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `manager` (String) Package manager to use: `"apt"`, `"dnf"`, `"yum"` or `"apk"`. `"auto"` uses the first of them whose tools are installed, in that order. Defaults to `"auto"`.
- `remove_on_destroy` (Boolean) Whether destroying the resource removes the package, if `state` is `"present"` or `"latest"`. Set to `false` for packages that must stay installed, such as ones that were installed before Terraform managed them. Defaults to `true`.
- `state` (String) `"present"` installs the package if it is missing (the newest available version, unless `version` is set); `"latest"` also upgrades it whenever the package index has a newer version; `"absent"` removes it. Defaults to `"present"`.
- `update_cache` (Boolean) During apply, refresh the package index (`apt-get update`, `dnf makecache`, `yum makecache`, `apk update`) before installing or upgrading the package, and always before checking for upgrades with `state = "latest"`; refresh during plan never updates it. The index is refreshed at most once per provider run, however many resources set this. Needed on fresh container images, which ship without an index. Defaults to `false`.
- `version` (String) Exact version to install, upgrading or downgrading the installed package to it, in the form the package database reports: `[epoch:]upstream[-revision]` for apt (`"2.10-3build1"`), `[epoch:]version-release` for dnf and yum (`"2.2.1-1.fc42"`; the release is required), `version-rN` for apk (`"2.2.1-r0"`). Only allowed with `state = "present"`. If unset, any installed version is accepted.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).
- `installed_version` (String) Version of the installed package, as reported by the package database; null if the package is not installed.

## Package Managers

With `manager = "auto"`, the default, the provider uses the first package manager whose tools it finds in `PATH`:

| `manager` | Distributions | Tools needed | Queries | Changes |
|-----------|---------------|--------------|---------|---------|
| `apt` | Debian, Ubuntu | `apt-get`, `apt-cache`, `dpkg-query` | `dpkg-query --show`, `apt-cache policy` | `apt-get install`, `apt-get remove`, `apt-get update` |
| `dnf` | Fedora, RHEL 8 and later, Rocky, Alma (dnf 4 and dnf 5) | `dnf`, `rpm` | `rpm --query`, `dnf check-update` | `dnf install`, `dnf downgrade`, `dnf upgrade`, `dnf remove`, `dnf makecache` |
| `yum` | Older RHEL-like distributions | `yum`, `rpm` | `rpm --query`, `yum check-update` | as for `dnf` |
| `apk` | Alpine | `apk` | `apk info`, `apk version` | `apk add`, `apk del`, `apk update` |

Every command runs directly, with an argument vector and never through a shell, with a 30-minute timeout (2 minutes for queries). The environment is the provider's own plus `LC_ALL=C`, so that output can be parsed, and `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive`, `DEBCONF_NONINTERACTIVE_SEEN=true`, `APT_LISTCHANGES_FRONTEND=none`, `APT_LISTBUGS_FRONTEND=none`, `UCF_FORCE_CONFFOLD=1` and `NEEDRESTART_MODE=l`, so that nothing prompts. With apt, configuration files you changed are kept (`--force-confdef --force-confold`), and a dpkg lock held by another process, such as `unattended-upgrades`, is waited for for up to 5 minutes.

Terraform applies independent resources in parallel, but package managers lock their database. The provider therefore runs one package command at a time, so several `sysutils_package` resources never fail each other's lock.

## Behavior

### Create and Update

The provider reads the package database, then:

- `state = "present"` without `version` installs the package if it is not installed. An installed package of any version is left alone.
- `state = "present"` with `version` installs exactly that version if a different one, or none, is installed: `apt-get install --allow-downgrades <name>=<version>`, `dnf install <name>-<version>` followed by `dnf downgrade` if a newer version stayed installed, or `apk add <name>=<version>`. With apk, the version constraint is also recorded in `/etc/apk/world`, so `apk upgrade` keeps it; apt and dnf do not hold the package, but the next plan reverts any upgrade.
- `state = "latest"` installs the package, or upgrades it if the package index has a newer version.
- `state = "absent"` removes the package if it is installed. apt and dnf also remove the packages that depend on it, as `apt-get remove` and `dnf remove` do; apk leaves a package that another one depends on installed, and the apply then fails, saying so.

With `update_cache = true`, the package index is refreshed first, but only if something is to be installed or upgraded, or `state` is `"latest"`, and at most once per provider run however many resources set it.

Afterwards the provider reads the package database again and fails if the result is not what was asked for, even if the package manager reported success. That catches virtual package names, for which apt installs a package with a different name, and held, excluded or pinned packages that are silently left alone. `installed_version` is set from the database.

If the package manager fails during create, the resource is still recorded, as tainted, so that the next apply or destroy can clean up a half-installed package.

### Destroy

If `state` is `"present"` or `"latest"` and `remove_on_destroy` is `true`, the package is removed if it is installed. Destroying a resource with `state = "absent"` or `remove_on_destroy = false` changes nothing.

Removing a package that another installed package needs removes that package too with apt and dnf; with apk, the package stays installed and destroy fails. Set `remove_on_destroy = false` for packages that must outlive the resource, such as `openssh-server`, or ones that were installed before Terraform managed them.

## Validation

`name` and `version` are checked at plan time, so that they can never be taken for an option, a shell word, a glob or a version constraint:

- `name` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._+-]{0,127}$`. With apt, it must also follow Debian's rules: lowercase, at least 2 characters, no `_`. Architecture qualifiers such as `:i386`, file paths and `provides` expressions such as `python3dist(foo)` are not accepted.
- `version` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9.+~^:_-]{0,127}$`, and the format of the manager: `[epoch:]upstream[-revision]` with an upstream version starting with a digit for apt, `[epoch:]version-release` for dnf and yum, `version-rN` for apk. It must be written as the package database reports it, which `installed_version` shows. An epoch of `0:` is the same as none.
- `version` is only allowed with `state = "present"`.

With `manager = "auto"`, the manager-specific rules are checked when the manager is known, at the start of the apply.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the package database, so that changes made with the package manager outside Terraform show up in the plan:

- If the package is not installed, `state` becomes `"absent"`, and the plan shows it changing back to `"present"` or `"latest"`. The next apply installs the package again.
- If a package with `state = "absent"` is installed, `state` becomes `"present"`, and the next apply removes it.
- If `version` is set and a different version is installed, `version` shows the installed version, and the next apply installs the configured one.
- With `state = "latest"`, if the package index has a newer version than the installed one, `state` becomes `"present"`, and the next apply upgrades the package. Refresh does not update the package index itself: it would slow down every plan and change the host during a plan. Newer versions therefore show up once the index has been refreshed, by `update_cache` on an apply, by a timer such as `apt-daily.timer`, or by dnf's automatic metadata refresh.

## Import

An installed package can be imported by name:

```shell
# By name. The package must be installed; it is imported with
# state = "present" and no version.
terraform import sysutils_package.nginx nginx
```

The package is imported with `state = "present"`, `manager = "auto"`, `remove_on_destroy = true` and without `version`. The import fails if the package is not installed. If your configuration sets `version` or `state = "latest"`, the first plan shows what the next apply changes.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root.
- It cannot be used with the provider's `root_dir` argument: package managers act on the running host, so the resource refuses to plan when `root_dir` is set. Use a separate provider configuration without `root_dir` for it.
- Only packages from the configured repositories can be installed, not local `.deb`, `.rpm` or `.apk` files. Repositories, keys, holds and version locks are not managed.
- With several architectures of a package installed (Debian multiarch, RPM multilib), the version of the first one the database lists is reported.
- The provider never answers questions a package asks during installation, such as debconf questions; the defaults are used. Preseed answers with `debconf-set-selections` in a [`sysutils_exec`](./exec.md) resource beforehand if you need others.
- Services installed by a package may be started by its installation scripts, as when you run the package manager yourself. Manage them with [`sysutils_systemd_unit`](./systemd_unit.md) or `systemctl`.
